    #160274. How to Prune a Christmas Tree – Fix a Too-Tall, Too-Wide, or Lopsided Tree for the Perfect Shape

    📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2284 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Gardeningknowhow ↗ Open Full Page

    How to Prune a Christmas Tree – Fix a Too-Tall, Too-Wide, or Lopsided Tree for the Perfect Shape

    📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2284 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

    ⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Unless you’re willing to settle for an artificial Christmas tree, you’re unlikely to find one that’s perfectly symmetrical.
    • It has been revealed that all of the best Christmas tree care in the world won’t help with these shaping issues.
    • It has been revealed that of course, knowing how to pick a Christmas tree with a good natural shape can save you some work in the first place.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Unless you’re willing to settle for an artificial Christmas tree, you’re unlikely to find one that’s perfectly symmetrical. We've all been there: you choose one that looks promising at the lot, then get it home and discover it's too tall or wide for your living room – or simply looks much more awkwardly shaped than you remembered. It’s enough to make you open the bottle of sherry you left out for Santa.

    It has been revealed that all of the best Christmas tree care in the world won’t help with these shaping issues. But a little careful pruning can make a big difference. Here, we will explain the steps to trim a too-tall, too-wide, or lopsided Christmas tree into a balanced, attractive centerpiece. We’ll also lay out the tools you need and the techniques you should use.

    It has been revealed that of course, knowing how to pick a Christmas tree with a good natural shape can save you some work in the first place. Before you begin trimming, remember that removing branches is much easier than putting them back. Work gradually, and try repositioning or fluffing branches before reaching for your pruners.

    A beautifully shaped Christmas tree should have a straight central trunk, a strong top branch to support a star or angel, and evenly spaced branches that create a full, balanced appearance.

    Recent findings suggest that commercial Christmas tree growers tend to encourage the classic conical Christmas tree shape through occasional pruning. They aim for a base width of around 60 to 70 percent of the tree's height, although a slimmer tree may be more practical for smaller rooms.

    Branch density matters, too. Large gaps between branch tiers can make a tree look sparse, while more closely spaced tiers create a fuller appearance – though denser branch tiers mean less space to hang ornaments.

    The first step, once you bring the new tree into your home, is to make a fresh, straight cut about half an inch (1.3 cm) from the base of the trunk. Some sellers will do this for you before you load it into your car, but it needs to be fresh. If you're doing it yourself, a pruning saw, like Fiskars' Pro 10-Inch Pruning Saw, available on Amazon, will make the job easier. Then, put the tree straight into a sturdy container of water. This is one of the most notable steps to make your Christmas tree last longer and prevent premature needle drop.

    Let the tree settle before doing any further trimming. Give the tree a few hours, or ideally overnight, to relax its branches. This is particularly important if the tree has been tightly wrapped in netting. Its branches need time to spread back into their natural positions, and what initially looks like an awkward gap or uneven section may become much less noticeable.

    According to recent reports, once the branches have relaxed, walk around the tree and look at it from several angles. Identify any protruding branches, bare patches, or uneven growth before deciding what actually needs cutting.

    You’ll need clean, sharp tools to prune a real Christmas tree into a pleasing cone shape. With the right tools and techniques, you can create a full, appealing tree no matter how tall, wide, or wonky it started out.

    Sources indicate that you can buy a hundred different tools for pruning trees, but you really don’t need more than a handful to prune a real Christmas tree. For smaller branches, a pair of budget-friendly pruners, like Fiskars Bypass Pruning Shears, will give you the control needed to make clean, precise cuts. For thicker branches, use loppers, like Corona ComfortGEL Bypass Loppers, which provide extra cutting power.

    For cutting through the trunk, use a sharp pruning saw or handsaw. Make sure the cut is straight so the tree sits securely in its stand.

    According to recent reports, is your Christmas tree too tall for your space? That’s usually one of the easiest Christmas tree problems to deal with, so don’t fret. First, measure your ceiling height, then subtract the height you need for the tree stand and tree topper, plus at least 1–2 inches (2.5–5 cm) of clearance. This is the perfect height for your fresh tree. Then measure the tree to see how much you need to remove.

    In a recent development, if you only need a modest reduction (say, a few inches), cut the excess length from the bottom of the trunk. Just make sure enough bare trunk remains to fit securely into the stand without forcing the lower branches against its rim. Then put the tree into its stand – ideally one with a built-in water reservoir, like the Krinner Genie Christmas Tree Stand.

    If your tree is significantly too tall, removing a large section of the trunk could also mean losing its attractive lower branches. In this case, you may need to shorten the central leader at the top instead. This is the upright shoot that forms the tree's tip.

    Sometimes the leader is disproportionately tall and can easily be shortened without spoiling the tree's shape. Other times, cutting off the original tip can ruin its natural outline and remove the little knobbly buds and side shoots that help hold a tree topper in place. Indeed, it might be better to go without a topper rather than making a drastic cut. So treat trimming the tip of your Christmas tree as a last resort, and only if you think it will work with its natural shape.

    According to recent reports, if you do decide to take this step, trim the leader carefully to the desired height. Then assess the tree's fresh shape and, if necessary, selectively shorten the surrounding branches until you achieve a symmetrical, conical outline. Work gradually, stepping back regularly to check your progress.

    Sources indicate that when a tree is too wide to fit gracefully in your home, you can trim its branches. A traditionally shaped Christmas tree has a base width of around two-thirds its height. But it’s a good idea to measure the floor space where the tree will stand to make sure that the “ideal” shape will work for you.

    Start by positioning the tree where you want it to stand and turning it to find the most attractive side. If branches at the back prevent it from fitting neatly against the wall, trim these first. Then, look at the tree from the front and sides, shortening any branches that stick out too far or spoil its overall shape.

    Work gradually, removing a little at a time, and step back often to check the results. You don't need to trim every branch to the same length – the aim is to create a balanced, natural-looking tree that fits comfortably in its space.

    For branches that genuinely need shortening, make cuts within the green, needle-covered portion of the growth. Avoid cutting too deeply into the bare, woody sections, as this can leave obvious gaps in the foliage that won't fill out.

    Recent findings suggest that remember that different types of Christmas trees naturally have different shapes. Some firs have a dense, compact outline, while certain spruces and pines have more open branching. Work with the tree's natural form rather than trying to force every variety into exactly the same silhouette.

    Industry observers note that it’s easier to talk about a too-tall or too-wide Christmas tree than one that’s just kind of weird. Whether it's lopsided or just plain wonky, you can still improve that uneven Christmas tree shape to make it presentable.

    Industry observers note that first, check that the trunk is standing straight in its base. Sometimes a tree that looks lopsided simply needs adjusting in the stand rather than pruning.

    To shape a lopsided Christmas tree, keep a cone shape in the front of your mind. Prune the upper branches shorter than the lower ones, and remember that the base width should be about two-thirds the tree's height. To achieve these goals, keep stepping back to see how things look.

    Industry observers note that take off any dead or damaged branches, then clip back any that protrude too far and spoil the tree's outline. If one side is particularly dense, you can selectively shorten a few branches to create a more balanced appearance. Work gradually, as it's easy to remove too much.

    It has been revealed that some unevenness comes from the way the tree grew. Christmas trees produce successive tiers of branches as they develop, and the amount of growth between these tiers influences how dense or open the finished tree appears. If one section has widely spaced branches, pruning alone won't necessarily make it look fuller.

    In a recent development, start by fluffing nearby branches or gently repositioning longer ones to disguise any gaps. You can also fold flexible branches into place and secure them with twine. If one side is woefully sparse, turn the tree so that this side is against the wall.

    It has been revealed that alternatively, you can borrow a branch from a particularly dense area of the tree and use it to fill an obvious gap. Simply cut the branch and secure it to the trunk or a sturdy neighboring branch with green wire, like this Pauleen floral wire from Amazon, positioning it to blend in with the surrounding foliage. Make sure it's firmly attached before adding any decorations.

    It has been revealed that if you'd rather not cut branches from elsewhere on your tree, artificial Christmas tree filler branches or greenery picks can work just as well. Look for ones that closely match the color and texture of your tree's needles, like these Hananona faux pine branches, and tuck them into sparse areas to create a fuller, more balanced appearance.

    You may also be able to disguise a sparse section by trimming back some of the heavier surrounding growth, helping the branches appear more evenly distributed. However, avoid cutting away too much greenery in an attempt to fill a gap – you could end up creating another one.

    It has been revealed that the only time you have to worry about a tree’s health is when it is alive. If you have a cut Christmas tree, it is no longer growing. That means that you do not have to worry about its health. Instead, trim the tree to fit well and look nice in your home.

    However, excessive Christmas tree shearing can still affect its appearance and stability. Removing too many lower branches may leave the trunk exposed, while cutting away large sections of the crown can make it difficult to achieve a natural shape.

    If, however, you buy a living Christmas tree you wish to plant, you do have to worry about keeping the tree healthy. Over-trimming can send the tree into shock or even kill it. The general rule is never to take off more than a quarter of the foliage annually. For most trimmings, stick to 10 percent.

    Don't cut conifers back to the woody inner branches. Most will not sprout new needles from these branches. Limit your pruning to green, needle-bearing growth. The only exception is if you remove an entire branch back to the trunk.

    If you're growing your own Christmas tree in the garden or keeping a living tree to use again in future years, pruning requires a different approach. Unlike a cut tree, a living evergreen needs to maintain healthy growth and develop a strong, balanced structure.

    Sources indicate that young Christmas trees generally need only light corrective pruning during their first few years. This might involve removing damaged branches, correcting an uneven shape, or dealing with two competing upright shoots. Ideally, the tree should have one dominant central leader to maintain a straight trunk and a natural pointed crown.

    In a recent development, more regular shaping can begin as the tree becomes established, often around its third growing season. For many Christmas tree species, growers carry out their main shearing once the new shoots have finished extending but before the fresh growth becomes fully firm. The timing varies according to the species and growing conditions.

    For a living Christmas tree you hope to keep for years, though, it's best to prune conservatively. Focus on correcting problems rather than heavily shearing the entire tree, and always check the pruning requirements of the particular species you're growing.

    Industry observers note that many people get overexcited when they start pruning a Christmas tree and are shocked to find out they have cut off too much. If this is you, take a breath. It’s only a Christmas tree. Resist the temptation to keep cutting elsewhere to even things up. A few strategically placed decorations will usually disguise the problem more effectively than further pruning.

    If you have snipped a few times too many and created a bare spot (or two!), here are a few tips for covering up the damage:.

    As you move through the necessary pruning, you’ll want to keep these few key rules in mind:.

She has studied horticulture and written about nature, trees, plants and gardening for more than two decades. Before turning her focus to gardening, she worked as an attorney and legal writer, experience she also brings to her role as our Gardening Lawyer. Her extended family includes some 30 houseplants and hundreds of outdoor plants, including 250 trees, which are her main passion. Spengler currently splits her life between San Francisco and the French Basque Country, though she was raised in Alaska, giving her experience of gardening in a range of climates.

    Industry News: Want To Befriend A Woodpecker? Here Are 6 Easy Ways To Attract These Striking Birds To Your Yard

    📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (962 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Long tied to forest and earth deities, woodpeckers are some of the most fascinating (and symbolically-laden) birds to welcome into your backyard.
    • That's right, folks; the birth month bird for August babies everywhere, the woodpecker represents curiosity, persistence, and determination.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Long tied to forest and earth deities, woodpeckers are some of the most fascinating (and symbolically-laden) birds to welcome into your backyard.

    That's right, folks; the birth month bird for August babies everywhere, the woodpecker represents curiosity, persistence, and determination. (And don't even get us started on what it means if they're the first bird you spot on January 1st!).

    Recent findings suggest that whether you believe in that or not, though, there's no denying that woodpeckers are considered one of the world's most popular birds for a reason... so, yes, it makes sense you'd like to befriend one!

    Oh sure, they might seem like woodland-only visitors, but there are actually several things you can do to encourage woodpeckers into your yard. In fact, whether you're hoping to spot a great spotted woodpecker, downy woodpecker, or another local species, a few simple changes can make your outdoor space a more welcoming place.

    Suet is one of the easiest foods to use to attract woodpeckers, especially during colder months when birds need extra energy and natural food sources become harder to find. Make sure, though, that you use a sturdy suet feeder designed to allow clinging birds to feed comfortably, and position it somewhere quiet where birds feel safe.

    You should also take care to choose quality suet cakes (you want the kind with seeds or nuts in!) and keep feeders clean. It may take a wee bit of time and patience for woodpeckers to discover your upcoming offering, but once they find a reliable food source, they may return regularly.

    Industry observers note that suet isn't the only food worth serving, as woodpeckers also enjoy peanuts and sunflower seeds, particularly black oil sunflower seeds, so long as you pop them in the sort of feeders that allow woodpeckers to perch or cling while feeding. (They don't like it one bit when you scatter food across the ground).

    As ever, we must stress that you should never offer salted or flavored nuts to wildlife.

    It has been revealed that it's all well and good teasing them in, but if you want woodpeckers to stick around, you need to think beyond feeders. And the best way to do this? By planting trees that provide insects, places to forage and shelter in abundance, of course!

    Recent findings suggest that take care to choose a tree that suits your available space and growing conditions, and remember that even a young tree can contribute to a more wildlife-friendly garden over time. Something like an oak is an excellent long-term habitat investment, while a birch offers lots of opportunities for birds to search for insects.

    A smaller ornamental tree that offers spring flowers, berries for birds, and beautiful fall color is also a good option for gardens with less room. Something like a serviceberry could work really well!

    Shop Woodpecker-Friendly Trees:.

    Recent findings suggest that I've said it before and I'll say it again, but a perfectly tidy garden isn't necessarily the most wildlife-friendly one. Dead branches, logs and tree stumps might not be the prettiest to look at (although that's changing; they've been stealing the spotlight at the RHS Chelsea Flower Show across the pond for years) but they can provide valuable habitat for insects and other invertebrates that woodpeckers forage for.

    Sources indicate that if you have a dead tree or limb that can safely remain, then, consider leaving it in place rather than removing it automatically. You could also create a small log pile or stumpery in a quiet corner of your yard. As the wood decays, it can add visual interest and become a bug buffet for woodpeckers and other birds.

    If you'd love to attract green woodpeckers in particular, consider giving your lawn a little more freedom, as these birds are particularly fond of ants ; in fact, they love nothing more than to use their long tongues to dig into nests and crevices to sccop them out and gobble them up.

    It has been revealed that avoid pesticides, then, and leave a patch of grass to grow longe if you can. You don't need to abandon lawn care completely, but creating a less manicured patch? It will encourage much more natural wildlife activity.

    In a recent development, just like other backyard birds, woodpeckers need fresh water for drinking and bathing. A shallow birdbath with gently sloping sides is a must, then, especially during hot weather or when natural water sources freeze.

    Recent findings suggest that be sure to pop it somewhere relatively quiet, with nearby trees or shrubs where birds can retreat if startled, but without dense cover immediately beside it where predators might lurk. A fine balance to strike, but a vital one, as I'm sure you'll agree.

    In a recent development, look, attracting woodpeckers isn't about transforming your yard overnight. By providing reliable food, planting trees, preserving natural habitat and offering fresh water, though, you can make your outdoor space a place where wildlife feels welcome. And when that distinctive drumming or flash of color finally catches your eye? Well, then you'll know the effort was all worth it.

    Kayleigh is an enthusiastic (sometimes too enthusiastic!) gardener and has worked in media for over a decade. She previously served as digital editor at Stylist magazine, and has written extensively for Ideal Home, Woman & Home, Homes & Gardens, and a handful of other titles. Kayleigh is passionate about wildlife-friendly gardening, and recently cancelled her weekend intends to build a mini pond when her toddler found a frog living in their water barrel. As such, her garden – designed around the stunning magnolia tree at its centre – is filled to the brim with pollinator-friendly blooms, homemade bird feeders, and old logs for insects to nest in.

    #160272. Industry News: Finding the Right Clients

    📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2398 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Finehomebuilding ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: Finding the Right Clients

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2398 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Finehomebuilding

    ⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that I spend a lot of time talking with builders who tell me they don’t really do marketing.
    • My first response is usually that this is a good thing.
    • Industry observers note that but I have also seen construction companies reach a point where the business landscape has changed, and reputation alone is not leading to the right clients.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that I spend a lot of time talking with builders who tell me they don’t really do marketing. Usually they say it with pride: “We’ve never had to. All of our work comes from word of mouth.”.

    My first response is usually that this is a good thing. If you’ve spent years building a company where past clients, architects, and trade partners keep sending work your way, you’ve built something valuable. In construction, reputation matters, and that kind of trust is earned over time. I would never tell a builder to replace that with advertising.

    Industry observers note that but I have also seen construction companies reach a point where the business landscape has changed, and reputation alone is not leading to the right clients. Good builders often struggle because the right people don’t know they exist.

    The phone may still be ringing, but the work coming in doesn’t always match where the manufacturer wants to go next. The business has evolved, but what people know about it hasn’t necessarily evolved with it.

    Recent findings suggest that those are the moments when someone usually states, often a little reluctantly, “I guess we need to do some marketing.” That may indeed be the case. But I think there is a simpler and more useful way to frame the problem: Are you known for the work you actually want to do? That is where I would start.

    According to recent reports, I’ve spent more than 20 years helping businesses and organizations grow, evolve, and connect with the people they want to reach, from owning and running a design and marketing agency to leading a destination marketing organization and working across marketing, branding, organizational leadership, consulting, and coaching. Today, as director of marketing and a business consultant with HELM Construction Solutions, I bring those experiences together in my work with builders, helping them think about where their business is going, the work they want more of, and what makes them different.

    Sit across the table with an experienced builder and you promptly understand what makes them different. But if you haven’t had that conversation, how would you know? I see this all the time: Some of the most valuable things about a construction company live almost entirely in the owner’s head. The challenge is making more of that knowledge visible.

    Industry observers note that before I talk with a builder about websites, social media, advertising, or anything else that might get labeled “marketing,” I want to understand the business they are trying to build. What kind of work would they happily do again? Which projects are profitable? Which projects make the crew proud? Which clients trust the process? Where do they want to work? Who do they want to work alongside? What do they want the organization to look like in five years? And—just as important—what do they want less of?

    That last question can be surprisingly provocative. Construction companies are often encouraged to think about growth only in terms of more: more projects, more employees, more revenue, more leads. But growth doesn’t always mean more projects. Sometimes it means being more intentional about the work you take on.

    Recent findings suggest that I’ll ask why a builder does something a certain way, and suddenly we’re deep into a story about a detail, a process, or a hard-earned lesson that changed how they work. Those stories are usually where the good stuff is, and where what makes a company different becomes clear.

    It has been revealed that at this point, a lot of decisions get easier. You don’t need to reach everybody. You just need to become more visible to the people who value that kind of work.

    If you aren’t sure how to identify the right types of projects for your business, I often suggest looking backward before looking forward. Choose three to five projects from the last few years that you would happily do again. Think about the jobs where the fit was right—the client trusted you, the work suited the strengths of your crew, the project was financially healthy, and the architect or designer was collaborative. Problems came up, as they always do, but the team solved them together rather than turning on one another. When the project ended, you were proud not only of what you built but of how you built it.

    Sources indicate that then ask a simple question: How did that project find us? You may discover that the same architect appears several times. Maybe a handful of past clients have been quietly sending people your way for years. Perhaps one designer, Realtor, supplier, or fellow builder keeps connecting you to projects that are an unusually good fit. Those patterns matter. They show you where to focus your time and attention. And when you’re trying to become known somewhere new, that kind of focus becomes even more key.

    Recent findings suggest that for example, Sycamore Builders in western North Carolina has strong experience with architect-led custom homes in mountain communities. But as the tech giant looks to expand into nearby markets, it faces a familiar challenge: Reputation is local.

    In some of those communities, builders have been around for generations. Their trucks are familiar. Realtors and architects know them. Their projects are part of the landscape. That familiarity has been built over years. You cannot advertise your way into a 25-year relationship.

    So Sycamore is taking a patient approach by building relationships with architects and Realtors, sharing more of the stories behind its work, and showing up consistently in a few specific communities. The goal isn’t a flood of calls. One or two well-aligned latest builds a year can make a ­meaningful difference.

    According to recent reports, if the word marketing makes you want to stop reading, forget about marketing for a minute. Take an hour with your business partner, project manager, or someone who knows your company well and work through these questions. Let your answers guide you in pinpointing the type of work you want to find. Once you do, you won’t need to network every week, post every day, or constantly upgrade your website. Pick a few actions that fit your business, and keep doing them.

    What work do people call you for—and what work do you wish people called you for?

    Recent findings suggest that be honest with yourself. Is the work you’re doing now the work you want to be doing? If not, that’s your starting point.

    What are five projects you’d do again tomorrow?

    In a recent development, what made those projects good for the client, the crew, and the business? Writing the answers down can help you determine the type of work you want to do more of.

    How did each of those projects find you?

    Maybe it was a past client, an architect, a builder, a Realtor, a jobsite sign, a Google search, or something else. Don’t guess—find out. Then you can use those same methods to find similar projects in the future.

    Who is connected to the work you want?

    In a recent development, make a list of the Realtors, architects, designers, and trade partners who are connected to the kinds of projects and clients you want more of, using your favorite projects as a guide. Who do you already know? Who consistently connects you to good-fit work? Who would you like to build a stronger relationship with?

    How can you stay connected to those people?

    Recent findings suggest that could you invite someone to a jobsite, meet for coffee, share an interesting project over email, attend an industry event, or simply check in occasionally? Staying in touch helps potential partners remember you and your business when the right project comes along.

    When someone looks you up, can they see what you want to be known for?

    Recent findings suggest that do your website and social media show the types of projects you want to do? Are you telling the stories behind that work and making your expertise visible? The clearer you are about the work you want, the easier it is for the right clients and partners to recognize that you’re the right fit.

    It has been revealed that this is usually the point where someone states, “Carrie, I have houses to build. I can’t spend all my time updating a website, posting on social media, meeting architects for coffee, and telling project stories.”.

    That’s fair, and I don’t want you to. Go back to what you learned about your best projects, and choose two or three things you can realistically keep doing to continue getting this sort of work. For example, maybe that means staying connected to a small group of architects and adding a strong project story to your website every few months.

    Then pay attention to what happens. Ask every latest caller how they heard about you, notice which relationships lead to good-fit projects, and see whether the work coming through the door starts to look more like the work you want.

    In a recent development, for example, longtime high-performance builder Steve DeMetrick of DeMetrick Housewrights has spent more than two decades developing a reputation for building homes that demonstrate thoughtful craftsmanship, durability, and energy-efficiency. Most of his work has come through referrals. He has deep expertise, strong relationships, and plenty of experience. He is not trying to make the phone ring more.

    Sources indicate that in fact, when we started talking about where he wants the organization to go next, his answer was almost the opposite of what we typically associate with growth. He wants to slow down. He wants fewer projects at a time, larger scope, deeper involvement with each client, earlier collaboration with architects, and more opportunity to use the knowledge he has accumulated over decades.

    The more we talked, the clearer it became that high-performance construction is only part of what makes his tech giant valuable. What really stands out is how he approaches the whole process—bringing design, budget, and scope together early and getting everyone working together sooner. That can lead to better decisions, fewer surprises, and a better experience for everyone involved. But that type of value is a lot harder to advertise on the side of a truck.

    Industry observers note that the goal isn’t simply to tell more people that DeMetrick Housewrights builds high-performance homes. It is to make more of Steve’s thinking visible, to tell the stories behind projects, to explain why he approaches preconstruction the way he does, and to give potential clients and collaborators a better sense of what it is actually like to work with him. The point isn’t to create content for the sake of content. It is to help people see expertise that is already there.

    Sources indicate that I’ve seen the same thing with Bell Street Builders in Maine, an employee-owned cooperative that does thoughtful restoration and renovation work around Portland and Casco Bay, including historic homes, architect-driven projects, and coastal and island construction. Those projects come with the kinds of challenges experienced builders know well: older structures that reveal surprises, coastal exposure, difficult logistics, complicated sequencing, and the need to make decisions carefully when clients may be living elsewhere.

    When I worked on Bell Street’s strategic direction, one theme kept reappearing: Bell Street knows old buildings. This is much more useful than generically saying the tech giant does “quality construction.”.

    In a recent development, if you own a 100-year-old house in Portland and are about to open walls that may be hiding decades of issues, you want a builder who understands what they’re looking at and can respond without turning every surprise into a crisis. If you’re an architect working on that house, you want a builder who can solve problems collaboratively and respect the building while still moving the project forward.

    Recent findings suggest that bell Street did not need to become known to every homeowner in southern Maine. The better opportunity was to become more recognizable for the work the firm does best and in the places where it wants to do more of it. That meant making sure its website and social channels indicated more of its historic work and the stories behind complex projects, staying connected with architects and designers who work on those kinds of homes, and building relationships in priority communities such as Portland’s West End, Foreside communities, and the Casco Bay islands.

    According to recent reports, becoming recognizable doesn’t have to mean constantly creating something new. One good project can go a long way. Document the challenges during construction, photograph the finished work, explain what the team had to solve, and share that story on a website, social media, or directly with architects and past clients who may know someone planning a similar project.

    I genuinely appreciate builders’ resistance to marketing. It usually stems from a belief that the work should matter most. I think so too.

    A clever website cannot make up for poor craftsmanship. Advertising cannot replace trust, and social media cannot substitute for treating clients well, running a good jobsite, respecting trade partners, or standing behind what you build. Your reputation still has to be earned.

    Sources indicate that once you’ve earned it, however, there is nothing wrong with helping it travel. That doesn’t require becoming a marketer. It simply means being a little more intentional about making the work, knowledge, and people behind your organization visible.

    It has been revealed that and there is a benefit beyond finding the kinds of projects you want. The same things that help clients, architects, designers, and trade partners understand your manufacturer also help potential employees understand it. Most builder websites show houses, but far fewer show the people behind them. A good carpenter who is considering their next move may want to know what kinds of projects they would work on, who they would work alongside, whether people stay, and whether there is room to grow.

    According to recent reports, make it easier for future employees and clients alike to understand who you are, what you do well, and where you’re headed. Because good work will lead to more good work, but only if people know about it.

    — Carrie Simmons is director of marketing and a business consultant at HELM Construction Solutions. Photo courtesy of HELM Construction Solutions.

    Latest Update: 7 Popular Garden Plants That Need Extra TLC Before Winter – Here's How to Protect Them From the Cold

    📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1467 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • With winter just around the corner, your garden is busy adjusting to the changes in light and temperature and, while some plants won’t fail to return next year, others are more vulnerable and need your help to survive.
    • According to recent reports, some of these garden stalwarts are tender perennials that simply won't survive outdoors in winter, while others are technically hardy but still a little vulnerable, so overwintering these plants well is vital.
    • Recent findings suggest that dahlias are some of the most varied and prized flowers of a late summer and fall garden, but they’re really only hardy in zones 8 through 11.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    With winter just around the corner, your garden is busy adjusting to the changes in light and temperature and, while some plants won’t fail to return next year, others are more vulnerable and need your help to survive. Many of our favorite flowering plants are the most susceptible to harm from changing temperatures, deep freezes and drying winter winds, so if you want lots of blooms again next year, give them the winter protection they need.

    According to recent reports, some of these garden stalwarts are tender perennials that simply won't survive outdoors in winter, while others are technically hardy but still a little vulnerable, so overwintering these plants well is vital. From protecting shrubs growing in the ground to digging bulbs up to take indoors, here's how to protect plants through winter so they wake up healthy in spring, ready for another bumper season of blooms.

    Recent findings suggest that dahlias are some of the most varied and prized flowers of a late summer and fall garden, but they’re really only hardy in zones 8 through 11. Their tuberous roots are susceptible to getting mushy in wet conditions and frozen in cold winter ground so leaving them in the ground is risky, especially in zones 6 and colder.

    Industry observers note that the best way to protect these plants for flowers next year is to lift dahlia tubers out of the ground after the first deep frost blackens the foliage. Cut the stems back to a couple inches, then carefully dig around and lift out the crown and tubers. Let these dry for a few days to cure and then store dahlia tubers in a box of wood shavings – a compressed bale of natural pet bedding such as this from Amazon is a cheap and convenient way to buy. Keep the box in a cool but frost-free, dry storage area such as an unheated garage, and you'll overwinter dahlias to replant next spring.

    Industry observers note that another plant that benefits from lifting is canna, which is only generally hardy in zones 7 through 10 because it grows from rhizomes that are vulnerable in freezing winter ground. Exact hardiness depends on the variety, so know your type and growing zone.

    According to recent reports, once the foliage has blackened after a frost, cut the stems back to four to six inches (10 to 15 cm) and then carefully dig up canna rhizomes to store for the winter. As with dahlias, it’s best to let these dry for a few days before storing them in a material like wood shavings. Overwinter canna rhizomes in a dark, cool and dry storage area until spring weather has warmed up enough to replant them outdoors.

    One of the most popular hydrangeas for its bright blue or pink flowers, bigleaf hydrangeas, also known as mophead hydrangeas, are typically hardy in zones 5 through 9. However, while the shrubs themselves cope with cold weather just fine, the problem with overwintering hydrangea shrubs that flower on old wood is the potential damage to next year’s flower buds that have developed before winter arrives. A cold snap can damage these buds, reducing the number of flowers you get next summer.

    To protect hydrangea buds, you’ll need to do more than simply covering the roots zone with mulch. Place four stakes in a square around the shrub and wrap burlap like this from Walmart for protection. In a very cold climate, increase the insulation by filling the space between the burlap and the plant with dry leaves.

    Industry observers note that hybrid tea roses can be hardy from zones 4 through 9, but there is some variation by cultivar, and they're still a little vulnerable to cold weather compared to other types of roses. So, to overwinter roses in a region with a harsh climate, give them some winter protection to ensure they make it through to spring in a healthy state, ready for strong growth.

    Your roses are vulnerable to damage caused by freeze-thaw cycles in the soil and winter damage to canes. First, clean up any plant debris on the ground to reduce the risk of disease, then loosely tie the canes together for extra support in damaging winter winds. Mound soil or compost around the base of the plant and for a final layer of insulation, top with a natural mulch such as Miracle-Gro All Natural Mulch, available from The Home Depot.

    In a recent development, rosemary is a Mediterranean herb that's generally hardy in zones 8 through 10. The best way to overwinter rosemary in colder climates is to bring it inside: trying to protect this plant outside with mulch is risky as it's very susceptible to wet, cold soil and drying winter winds. However, using a mulch is helpful in zones 7 or 8 to give the roots a little extra insulation.

    In colder areas, dig up your rosemary plant and move it into a pot that you can bring it indoors. Even better, grow rosemary in a pot year-round as it won’t appreciate being dug out of the ground once established. This Mediterranean herb is one of those plants that grow better in terracotta pots because of the well-drained conditions the porous clay walls create. And because the pot won't be left outside in freezing temperatures, a cheap terracotta planter like this from Lowe's is all you need.

    Recent findings suggest that rosemary doesn't tolerate soggy roots so to improve drainage, mix perlite like Back to the Roots Organic Perlite, available from Walmart, into any all-purpose potting mix at a ratio of 1:3. Indoors, give your potted plant a cool, bright spot and avoid overwatering.

    Sources indicate that species and varieties of Colocasia and Alocasia offer large, striking, tropical leaves in summer but are only hardy in zones 8 through 11. Elephant ears grow from corms (large underground structures similar to tubers) which should be dug up for winter in colder growing zones.

    Sources indicate that to store Elephant ear corms over winter, let the foliage die back after a frost, then cut back the stems and leaves. Dig around the corm and lift it from the ground, allowing it to dry for up to two weeks before storing in wood shavings in a cool, dry spot. If your Elephant ear is growing in a pot, and small enough, the other option is bring it indoors for winter. While some types can be kept actively growing to enjoy as a houseplant, it's more usual to trim and overwinter tropical plants indoors in a semi-dormant state in a bright but cool spot.

    In a recent development, many salvias are winter hardy up to zone 3, but in regions with cold winters, more tender varieties are usually grown as annuals. Alternatively, you can try to protect these tender salvia varieties like Brazilian sage or gentian sage from winter weather, and this strategy works best in borderline zones like 6 or 7.

    Sources indicate that to overwinter tender salvias outside, use a thick layer of an airy natural mulch such as long-needle pine straw mulch like this from Amazon around the root zone and crown. In a more exposed garden, bark chips like these Pine Mulch Nuggets, also from Amazon, are heavier but create the same airy conditions. Leave the stems in place as they're hollow and trap air that can help insulate the crown.

    If you're growing tender salvias in containers, simply bring them inside for the winter, placing them in a spot with bright light and reduce watering as growth will slow.

    In a recent development, timing for winter protection depends on the plant and your local climate and weather in your USDA zone. Tender plants should be brought inside before the first frost, but for plants that grow from tubers, rhizomes or corms that need lifting from the ground, wait until after the first deep frost.

    It has been revealed that for mostly hardy perennials that simply need a little protection to remain healthy outside, you need to strike a balance between acting before the ground freezes and waiting until the plant goes dormant. Insulating these plants from the cold by mulching or covering too early can delay dormancy and encourage growth that's quickly damaged once temperatures drop.

    Protecting your precious plants before winter arrives isn't complicated or difficult. You simply need to know what you're growing and how the plants tolerate your local winters, then protect them accordingly. A little effort now will reward you next year with strong new growth as soon as temperatures rise in spring, and an abundant display of flowers.

    According to recent reports, mary Ellen Ellis has been gardening for over 20 years. With degrees in Chemistry and Biology, Mary Ellen's specialties are flowers, native plants, and herbs.

    Latest Update: Margo Valdes, Weatherization Contractor

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (402 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Finehomebuilding

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that after years as a building-performance consultant, Margo Valdes grew frustrated of seeing the problems that arise when contractors ignore fundamental building science.
    • In a recent development, margo graduated from college with degrees in economics and physics, but her favorite course was “Castles,” taken during a semester abroad in England.
    • It has been revealed that after working an unfulfilling office job, Margo saw an ad for a HERS rater at Conservation Services Group (now CLEAResult).
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that after years as a building-performance consultant, Margo Valdes grew frustrated of seeing the problems that arise when contractors ignore fundamental building science. Three years ago, she founded Athena Building Performance, a weatherization tech giant built on the premise that getting the details right starts with understanding why a building behaves the way it does.

    In a recent development, margo graduated from college with degrees in economics and physics, but her favorite course was “Castles,” taken during a semester abroad in England. The class explored how to determine the age of a castle, identify the type of stone used to build it, and understand the reasoning behind its design. Margo loved it.

    It has been revealed that after working an unfulfilling office job, Margo saw an ad for a HERS rater at Conservation Services Group (now CLEAResult). The job sounded like a good fit, so she applied, and her career in building performance began.

    Margo spent about six years at CSG and credits the company with giving her a strong foundation in building science. Though her work as a HERS rater focused on testing and evaluating, she received hands-on training in air-sealing and choosing and installing insulation. After leaving CSG, Margo’s focus shifted from upcoming construction to existing buildings. She joined a consulting firm, where she spent seven years as director of the Existing Buildings team.

    Over the years, Margo became increasingly aware of how much the quality of weatherization work depends on understanding the building as a system—adding insulation affects moisture, and sealing air leaks changes ventilation. She decided the best way to improve the work was to get closer to it. That led her to the contractor side of the business, and to founding Athena.

    According to recent reports, today, Athena operates as a specialized weatherization contractor, tackling residential air-sealing and insulation upgrades. While Margo spends most of her time managing the business, knowledgeable practice remains at its heart: Every fresh hire spends weeks doing hands-on field training and diagnostic walk-throughs to understand not just how the work is done, but why.

    Industry observers note that margo envisions eventually expanding Athena into a full-service building-enclosure firm. For now, she’s focused on centering the company around what started it all: thoughtful, educated work.

    Dissolving Into the Forest

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (337 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Finehomebuilding

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • This home was designed with two main goals in mind.
    • Outside, three irregular, offset buildings—the main house, a sauna, and a garden shed—mimic the tree-filled landscape, while Nakamoto Forestry’s Gendai yakisugi charred-wood siding provides a darkened exterior reminiscent of the texture of tree bark.
    • It has been revealed that inside, the dark, textured exterior gives way to bright, airy interiors filled with natural light, lighter wood finishes, and carefully framed views.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    This home was designed with two main goals in mind. The first was for it to integrate into its forest setting, making it feel at home among the trees. The second was to capture forest views from a light-filled yet intimate interior. By focusing on these goals, the architects designed a home that feels less like an object in the forest than a place quietly woven into it.

    Outside, three irregular, offset buildings—the main house, a sauna, and a garden shed—mimic the tree-filled landscape, while Nakamoto Forestry’s Gendai yakisugi charred-wood siding provides a darkened exterior reminiscent of the texture of tree bark.

    It has been revealed that inside, the dark, textured exterior gives way to bright, airy interiors filled with natural light, lighter wood finishes, and carefully framed views. Because the living spaces are stacked to fill the irregular form of the main house, each room provides a unique view of the landscape, with windows that vary in scale.

    Large windows in the living room and a sliding glass door in the dining area allow in sunlight and views from different directions, the primary bedroom on the top floor includes a small north-facing window, and a large window next to the bathtub frames the view of an eastern hilltop.

    The design team used the height of the ceilings to guide the function of each space, with cathedral ceilings creating a spacious effect in the main living spaces, cozier sloped ceilings in the primary bedroom and bathroom, and a welcoming reading nook in the second-floor bedroom where the roof slope drops to a low kneewall.

    #160268. How to Design a Garden That Solves Problems and Invites You In

    📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1043 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Finegardening ↗ Open Full Page

    How to Design a Garden That Solves Problems and Invites You In

    📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1043 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Finegardening

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that people often ask how I approach the garden design process and what information I gather before developing a plan.
    • I like to create purpose-driven designs.
    • Design is all about solving problems and connecting clients to their gardens, usually beginning with a questionnaire to bring all those unspoken needs to light.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that people often ask how I approach the garden design process and what information I gather before developing a plan. While every client and garden is different, I usually start with the same basic questions.

    I like to create purpose-driven designs. For example, I’m often called on to solve a problem, even if it is simply “I have a new house and a blank slate.” It may be just a section of the garden, the front yard, or something specific like repairing a garden after a new septic system installation or after a new house is built next door.

    Design is all about solving problems and connecting clients to their gardens, usually beginning with a questionnaire to bring all those unspoken needs to light. Questions help people consider things they would not normally think about. As a result, these conversations define their needs and desires, helping me combine different elements into a cohesive design.

    The same approach applies to projects in my own garden. I don’t give myself a questionnaire, but I do ask myself the same questions. First, I assess the challenges, the location of the area in relation to the rest of the property, and the environmental conditions that will influence the planting.

    It has been revealed that in a latest garden, the major goal is often screening. Most people want privacy to live their lives outside without having to see a neighboring house, road, commercial area, or vacant lot.

    It has been revealed that privacy was one of the massive considerations when planning my grass garden. There was no privacy between my property and the neighboring property. I could see my neighbors eat their dinner, watch them play with their grandchildren, and even see them argue. Their house was also too close to the property line, and in fact, their sidewalk was on my property. That was a problem.

    Because the sidewalk was already there when I moved in, I had to incorporate it into my design, but I could still make it disappear visually.

    Industry observers note that I started out with some tall elements at the back of the bed to start the screening process. I positioned these plants so I could maintain them from my property without having branches extend over the property line. Keeping their mature size in mind also helped avoid potential conflicts with the neighboring property. Soft screens made of trees and tall shrubs (both evergreen and deciduous) offer privacy without creating a harsh, artificial boundary line.

    Read More: 20 Unique Hedging Plant Options.

    Sources indicate that looking at the space, I could see a definite focal point within my property. With the neighbor behind me, the view naturally led the eye toward the water. Therefore, I designed a one-sided border rather than an island bed meant to be viewed from multiple directions. Making the border as deep as 20 feet in places gave me enough room to continue screening the neighboring property while also providing some sound buffering.

    Industry observers note that understanding the environmental conditions was the next step. The back edge is on the north side of my property. The large trees and shrubs would not shade the rest of the bed. This meant the bed would be in full sun all day, all season long.

    What a challenge for this PNW native who grew up mostly in the forest (or woods, as we called it). I had to learn about plants that liked full sun, drying winds, and dry soil so they could thrive. Rather than trying to re-create the shaded woodland conditions I knew best, I needed to work with what the site naturally offered.

    Read More: Summer-Dry Gardening: A Visit to Beth Chatto’s Gravel Garden.

    In a recent development, growing up in the forest, I longed for wide-open sky and long views. Above all, I wanted to immerse myself in the garden. A long row of hedging plants that I could only look at wasn’t what I had in mind. I wanted to become part of the blowing, rustling movement of the grasses. While experiencing the plants, I also wanted to connect with insects, pollinators, birds, frogs, and even a few rabbits.

    I consider the challenge met. The amount of wildlife activity surrounding me in the garden never ceases to amaze me. I feel as if I’m in a different world while surrounded by all the action and movement of the grasses and perennials, far away from big cedar trees, moss, and ferns. Sun, wind, fragrant flowers, and the smell of warm earth are all-encompassing there.

    Even during the winter, this garden pulls me out, bundled up and coffee in hand, to see what is happening. Early spring bulbs push through the soil, mice shelter under the evergreen sedges, and birds search for a breakfast of grass seeds and gather bits and pieces to build fresh nests.

    The ultimate goal of any designer is finding the right outdoor elements to pull people outside and connect them with nature. Those elements are individual to each client. They could be an eating area, outdoor kitchen, hot tub, play area, pond, fountain, or hidden sitting area. Maybe the goal is plant-driven, with a vegetable garden, cutting garden, or collection of conifers.

    When these features are thoughtfully integrated with immersive, naturalistic plantings, the result is an outdoor space that invites people to experience their gardens throughout the year.

    And for more Pacific Northwest regional reports, click here.

    Susan Calhoun is the owner and principal designer of Plantswoman Design in Bainbridge Island, Washington.

    #160267. Same Footprint, More Function

    📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (319 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Finehomebuilding ↗ Open Full Page

    Same Footprint, More Function

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (319 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Finehomebuilding

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, the owners of this 1940s house wanted to add more space for a growing family, but site restrictions would only allow them to build upward, meaning the small home would tower over surrounding houses.
    • Outside, the remodeled house maintains the same proportions of the original but incorporates modern updates such as the ACRE composite-wood entry accents and the single entry-door sidelight.
    • According to recent reports, creating a more functional home within the same footprint means making the most of every inch of usable space.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, the owners of this 1940s house wanted to add more space for a growing family, but site restrictions would only allow them to build upward, meaning the small home would tower over surrounding houses. To preserve the house’s place in the neighborhood and keep costs down, the solution was to remodel the existing space with a more functional layout, transforming the second floor from two bedrooms and one bath into three bedrooms and two baths while making the home feel more spacious, flexible, and connected.

    Outside, the remodeled house maintains the same proportions of the original but incorporates modern updates such as the ACRE composite-wood entry accents and the single entry-door sidelight. To improve flow inside, the main staircase was relocated to create a more functional, open interior. Newly introduced sliding glass doors offer more light inside and a seamless connection to the outdoors, maximizing the feeling of space. The basement stairs are now accessed via a hidden floor hatch, preserving the open main living area.

    According to recent reports, creating a more functional home within the same footprint means making the most of every inch of usable space. The area under the main staircase now houses deep storage drawers, and a new window seat offers extra space next to the picture window.

    On the exterior, the window-seat bump-out lets the house live larger without increasing its footprint. Clad in the same wood as the front entry, the bump-out creates a cohesive and striking connection between the front and back of the house.

    Arianne and Micah’s Small Urban Minneapolis Garden

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (876 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Finegardening

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • I’ve recently gotten a few emails from readers asking about submissions they entered through the website link at the end of every GPOD.
    • Recent findings suggest that today we’re touring Arianne and Micah’s garden in Minneapolis, Minnesota.
    • Industry observers note that in Minneapolis, our growing season may be short, but we squeeze every drop of joy out of our small urban garden!
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, hi GPOD! I’ve recently gotten a few emails from readers asking about submissions they entered through the website link at the end of every GPOD. Unfortunately, I haven’t received any submissions through the form in quite a while. I’m not sure what the problem is, but hopefully there will be a resolution soon. In the meantime, you can submit your photos and captions through the email linked below instead.

    Recent findings suggest that today we’re touring Arianne and Micah’s garden in Minneapolis, Minnesota. And while looking through their latest photos, I kept forgetting that I was looking at a garden in the Midwest! Arianne has shared their garden with us before, and I’m excited to see what they’ve been growing this year. Here’s Arianne:.

    Industry observers note that in Minneapolis, our growing season may be short, but we squeeze every drop of joy out of our small urban garden! It’s packed with flowers I start from seed—like zinnias, cosmos, statice, strawflower, celosia, and amaranth—along with overwintered dahlias. I love cutting fresh bouquets to gift to friends, family, and coworkers. When we’re not admiring the blooms, my husband is cooking outdoors—making wood-fired pizzas, wok dishes, and hosting family birthday celebrations right in the heart of our cozy yard.

    It has been revealed that arianne packs plenty of interest into the garden along in the front yard and along the curb strip. Plants in this section of the garden include dwarf purple smokebush, threadleaf bluestar (Amsonia hubrichtii, Zones 5–8), boxwood (Buxus cvs., Zones 4–9), lamb’s ear (Stachys byzantina, Zones 4–8), purpleleaf sand cherry (Prunus × cistena, Zones 2–8), coreopsis (Coreopsis cvs., Zones 3–9), alliums (Allium cvs., Zones 3–9), sedum, and artemisia. It’s a great mix of foliage colors and textures even when everything isn’t in bloom.

    I love the placement of the patio and pathway. It’s a really useful design technique for maximizing every square inch of a small garden while still leaving plenty of room for outdoor living.

    Sources indicate that absolutely gorgeous section of the garden! This is where we really start to feel like we’re in the tropics. ‘Mars Madness’ hardy hibiscus (Hibiscus ‘Mars Madness’, Zones 4–9) has all the tropical drama while still being hardy enough for a Minneapolis winter. And it’s hard to miss those giant cannas and the colorful foliage on the coleus. I love all the red blooms too!

    One of Arianne’s fabulous container combinations features Tropicanna Gold canna (Canna ‘Mactro’, Zones 8–11), purple shield (Strobilanthes dyerianus, annual), begonias (Begonia cvs., annual), flowering kale (Brassica oleracea, annual), and parrot’s beak (Lotus berthelotii, annual). So much of the color and interest here comes from foliage!

    There is so much to look at in this section of the garden! Those variegated geranium leaves are striking, and I could go on and on about Arianne’s use of color and texture. The apple tree surrounded by all these ornamentals is an unexpected but lovely touch.

    Just around the corner from the photo above. Another gorgeous tropical container, and ‘Blue Shadow’ fothergilla (Fothergilla × intermedia ‘Blue Shadow’, Zones 5–8) grows on the left in this view.

    It has been revealed that another view of the backyard borders. There are so many plants packed into this garden, you would never believe this is a small urban backyard. And, if my eyes are working correctly, I’d say that’s a clover lawn?!

    According to recent reports, tall conifers create a fantastic privacy screen in this view. The garden really is its own secluded paradise.

    A shady combination of hostas, ‘Banana Boat’ sedge (Carex siderosticha ‘Banana Boat’, Zones 4–9), painted fern, purple shield, coleus, and impatiens.

    Recent findings suggest that zinnias, statice, amaranth, and overwintered dahlias are just some of the blooms that make their way into bouquets for friends, family, and coworkers. So pretty!

    It has been revealed that thank you so much for sharing your garden with us again, Arianne! It’s always a treat to see what you and Micah are growing, and I think I could spend hours wandering around this garden and still find something new to admire.

    📖 Baca

    Fall Color in Nancy’s Massachusetts Garden

    • Today we’re heading to Hingham, Massachusetts, for some beautiful fall color from Nancy.
    • This is our sugar maple (Acer saccharum, Zones 3–8) showing off its fall foliage before it drops its leaves to keep my gardens warm this winter.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, hi GPOD! Today we’re heading to Hingham, Massachusetts, for some beautiful fall color from Nancy. Nancy sent in photos of the trees and shrubs winding down the season in her garden, along with one of the last flowers still hanging on.

    This is our sugar maple (Acer saccharum, Zones 3–8) showing off its fall foliage before it drops its leaves to keep my gardens warm this winter.

    My ‘Forest Pansy’ eastern redbud (Cercis canadensis ‘Forest Pansy’, Zones 5–9) is maroon most of the year until fall, when it turns a lovely yellow.

    My paperbark maple (Acer griseum, Zones 4–8) has had a hard time coping with our summer droughts and water restrictions, but it looked a lovely red this fall.

    According to recent reports, this is another native tree that many people are not familiar with, fringe tree (Chionanthus virginicus, Zones 4–9), which has fragrant white flowers hanging from its branches in late spring to early summer. As you can see, it also looks beautiful in its yellow fall foliage.

    In the front of this picture is a young sweetgum (Liquidambar styraciflua, Zones 5–9), which has spectacular red color in the fall and develops spiky seed balls as it matures. In the distance is a blackhaw viburnum (Viburnum prunifolium, Zones 3–9) showing its orange fall color.

    ‘Mount Airy’ fothergilla (Fothergilla ‘Mount Airy’, Zones 5–8) glows red and orange in front of fragrant abelia (Abelia mosanensis, Zones 4–8), whose fall color is beginning to fade. The abelia will charm us all again in spring with its fragrant blooms.

    It has been revealed that sweetshrub (Calycanthus floridus, Zones 5–9) on the right has turned a lovely yellow. Amazingly, all three sweetshrubs shown here had the bark eaten off around every trunk by rabbits last winter, killing every one. They all grew back from the roots, showing just how resilient they are. On the left, ‘Mount Airy’ fothergilla is showing off its red fall foliage, and in back is ‘Alice’ oakleaf hydrangea (Hydrangea quercifolia ‘Alice’, Zones 5–9) with maroon fall foliage.

    One of the only flowers left blooming is ‘Sheffield Pink’ chrysanthemum (Chrysanthemum ‘Sheffield Pink’, Zones 5–9), which complements the dark foliage of Diabolo ninebark (Physocarpus opulifolius ‘Monlo’, Zones 3–7) behind it.

    Sources indicate that thanks for sharing your fall garden with us, Nancy! Nancy says she’s ready to wander the garden, make her list of what needs dividing in spring, and figure out what new plants need to be bought. Sounds like a good way to spend the off-season to me!

    Hi GPOD! Yesterday we enjoyed some beautiful fall color in Nancy’s Massachusetts garden, and today we’re heading west to see what fall looked like in Colorado this year.

    Bonnie took these photos in mid-November after an unusually long fall. While the trees certainly put on a show, Bonnie states the shrubs were the real stars this year. Here’s Bonnie:.

    Recent findings suggest that colorado put on a spectacular fall color display this year. My garden was filled with so many vivid hues that I had to capture them in photos. Some years are more colorful than others, and this was certainly a good one! The standout colors came not from the trees, but from the shrubs.

    Sources indicate that welcome to my fall garden! Just walk through the arch and see the colors beyond. ‘Forest Pansy’ eastern redbud (Cercis canadensis ‘Forest Pansy’, Zones 5–9) starts in spring with dark burgundy leaves, turns green by late summer, and finishes the season in bright yellow. I love this tree!

    Other stars in my fall garden are the barberries, hydrangeas, dwarf smokebushes (Cotinus coggygria cvs., Zones 4–8), and spireas. Oh, and the Diabolo ninebark (Physocarpus opulifolius ‘Monlo’, Zones 3–7) in the back turned a lovely red this year.

    Barberry, dwarf smokebush, and spireas in the back make a nice composition.

    Industry observers note that I’m in love with these ‘Annabelle’ smooth hydrangeas (Hydrangea arborescens ‘Annabelle’, Zones 3–9). They are all over my yard.

    Another hydrangea vignette with viburnum, boxwood, and Japanese forest grass (Hakonechloa macra, Zones 5–9) in front.

    I love the beautiful colors of this barberry.

    Around the other side of our yard, the dwarf smokebush shines among the evergreens and the orange leaves of the mountain ash and honey locust (Gleditsia triacanthos, Zones 3–8) trees.

    Looking toward the front yard, the dwarf smokebush steals the show!

    Another view from the front yard.

    A weeping Norway spruce (Picea abies, Zones 3–7) and barberry make a beautiful combination.

    Sources indicate that thanks for sharing your beautiful fall garden with us, Bonnie! The trees are gorgeous, but I agree that the shrubs really stole the show this year.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that A common theme in home design is the idea of blending the architecture with the landscape, allowing the building to sit lightly on the land. You might not expect a 4350-sq.-ft. modern home to be a shining example of how to achieve that goal, but this fresh modern home in Bend, Ore., balances a striking architectural presence with a remarkably light touch on the landscape below.

    The new building required enough space to house multiple generations, but maximum exposure to the meadow setting and mountain views meant siting the house on a hilltop. To meet both requirements while also only lightly interrupting the land, 40% of the home is set above grade, with a cantilevered great room that appears to float over the ground and that is supported by two special-ordered structural steel beams.

    It has been revealed that to further capitalize on the views, the common spaces feature expansive glazing, including a 40-ft. sliding glass wall, while roof overhangs allow the exterior to become part of the interior when large doors are open—while also providing shade and protection from the elements.

    Because the house might accommodate one or two people at some times and upwards of 10 at others, the floor initiative is broken up into both large and small common spaces. These include a great room centered around a concrete fireplace designed for larger groups, and a roof deck for more intimate gatherings.

    I have lived in this house and garden for a little over a year. When I moved here, I worked hard to transplant many of my plants, and the garden continues to be a work in progress.

    Delphinium (Delphinium cvs., Zones 3–7) with coleus (Coleus scutellarioides, annual).

    In a recent development, A work in progress… I transplanted this hearts-a-bustin’ (Euonymus americanus, Zones 6–9) from a different spot where I originally had it. It was crowded in and now will be able to spread out.

    This celosia (Spicata group) actually grew from seeds of plants that were in a pot last summer. The ground in this area is where a tree used to be, and the roots are rotting and creating wonderful soft soil.

    Sources indicate that thanks for sharing another revision from your garden, Connie! And I have to know: What variety of watermelon did your husband grow? It’s huge and oblong! I hope it was delicious. Looking forward to the next update! 🙂.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Hi GPOD! Longtime contributor Kielian is back today with another beautiful look at her garden in Hamilton, Montana. We’ve followed this garden through the seasons for years, and GPOD readers may even remember Kielian’s first autumn tour from more than a decade ago. Today she’s sharing what fall looks like on the ranch nearly 17 years into the garden’s evolution.

    In the Bitterroot Valley of Montana, fall imparts her special light and changing colors to the ranch. The gardens are closing in on 17 years of beauty and, interestingly, have decided which design they like the most… on their own.

    My detailed blueprints and drawings of plantings have been changed by Mother Nature, who knows so much more than I do about proper placement. Birds deposit valuable seeds in areas I would never have approved of, and the failure of certain plants to survive makes room for those that forge ahead with gusto. Ahh, autumn, how delightful are your colors and resilience.

    Late October in Montana: The ‘Pee Wee’ oakleaf hydrangeas (Hydrangea quercifolia ‘Pee Wee’, Zones 5–9) are showing off, and the ornamental pear tree was not going to be outdone.

    The front garden early in the morning: Shadows enhance the color changes.

    In a recent development, the back deck was sprinkled with maple-tree graffiti. The linden tree boasted brilliant yellow, and a gorgeous crabapple by the pump house screamed for attention with bright red leaves.

    A smokebush (Cotinus coggygria, Zones 4–8) and aspen tree drip with early morning rain.

    A golden sunset scattered early October rays on quaking aspens (Populus tremuloides, Zones 1–6), enhanced by the Bitterroot Mountains as a backdrop.

    Tessa came running along the path through early November changing leaves.

    In a recent development, an ornamental pear tree with fading black-eyed Susans in front. Winter is on her way.

    Thanks for sharing another season in your garden with us, Kielian! After seeing this garden in spring, summer, fall, and even covered in snow over the years, it’s hard to pick a favorite season. But that golden sunset over the pond with the Bitterroot Mountains in the distance certainly makes a strong case for fall!

    💡 Key Takeaways

    • I understand the reasons for not cutting down perennials and for letting leaves lie untouched over the winter, but it takes me about 10 weeks to clean up.
    • In a recent development, so I’ve been cleaning up, and the garden has been looking pretty bare recently, positively grim on overcast days.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that hey, garden gang! Longtime contributor Susan Warde is back today with a closer look at her garden in St. Paul, Minnesota. We’ve seen what the end of the season looks like in Susan’s garden before, but today she’s focusing on the smaller details that are easy to overlook this time of year.

    I understand the reasons for not cutting down perennials and for letting leaves lie untouched over the winter, but it takes me about 10 weeks to clean up. I have a large garden, family commitments, unpredictable weather, and a limited number of yard-waste bags that our pickup service will take at one time. Ten weeks in the spring would put me into mid-June before I could get the weeds and overwintered mess under control.

    In a recent development, so I’ve been cleaning up, and the garden has been looking pretty bare recently, positively grim on overcast days. But during the process I was struck by small vignettes of beauty that stood out in an otherwise desolate landscape.

    The underside of some Korean maple leaves (Acer pseudosieboldianum, Zones 4–8).

    A ‘Northern Hi-Lights’ azalea (Rhododendron ‘Northern Hi-Lights’, Zones 4–7) with bright fall color… and buds that promise spring.

    The seed head of ‘Guernsey Flute’ clematis (Clematis ‘Guernsey Flute’, Zones 4–9) that had a second late flowering.

    One last blossom on a ‘Max Frei’ bloody cranesbill (Geranium sanguineum ‘Max Frei’, Zones 3–8).

    Raindrops on columbine (Aquilegia cvs., Zones 3–8) leaves.

    The yellowed leaves of a bulblet fern (Cystopteris bulbifera, Zones 3–8) that I’d overlooked during the cutting-down process.

    A bee enjoys the very last plant in bloom, black cohosh (Actaea racemosa, Zones 3–8).

    Evergreen Christmas fern (Polystichum acrostichoides, Zones 3–8) and moss.

    I had never before looked closely at the bark of a blue beech (Carpinus caroliniana, Zones 3–9), which from a distance just looks taupe.

    Recent findings suggest that five minutes before taking the photo, I’d cleaned out this birdbath—the one I leave available in winter, and then only on above-freezing days. The leaves are from a ‘North Wind’ maple (Acer × pseudosieboldianum ‘IslNW’, Zones 4–7).

    Sources indicate that thanks for sharing these small moments from your garden, Susan! There are so many things to love about a garden, but I often find that the small details people tend to gloss over are even more reason to celebrate. There’s so much happening at once! You just have to look closely to see it. (:.
